title: Beatrix and the Portrait
premise: Theo Nakamura, a hardened skeptic and property surveyor, is hired to appraise the Aldergate house, a property whose rooms rearrange themselves and whose measurements never come out the same twice. When his excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside, they discover the house feeds on belonging: it keeps what it loves, and it loved a girl named Beatrix, who vanished in 1974 and has been waiting inside ever since. To escape, Theo must return what was stolen that year — Beatrix's portrait, hidden in the town archive by her own family — and choose between the loyalty that binds him to his crew and the truth that could free them all. On the night of the harvest moon, Theo burns the portrait inside the house, releasing Beatrix and collapsing the house's hungry heart; the survivors walk out at dawn, and the lot is appraised at exactly nothing.
about_author: Juniper Nakamura is the pen name of a former land surveyor who spent a decade measuring old houses across the Pacific Northwest before turning to horror. Their debut draws on field notes, county archives, and one house they refuse to name.

chapters.title: The Measurement That Wouldn't Hold
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Theo arrives at the Aldergate house for a routine appraisal, but every room measures differently on his second pass, and the hallway is eleven inches longer than it was at noon. His crew jokes about bad tape measures; Theo writes it off as settling foundations. The emotional beat is the comfort of rationality — and the first hairline crack in it.

chapters.title: What the Crew Unearthed
chapters.summary: POV Marisol, the excavation lead. Digging the new foundation line, the crew strikes a door — oak, iron-banded, sealed with hinges on the inside. When Marisol touches it, the ground exhales, and every worker hears their own name spoken from below. The beat is collective dread: something down there has been waiting to be found.

chapters.title: Beatrix, 1974
chapters.summary: POV Theo, interleaved with archival documents. Researching the property, Theo finds a 1974 missing-persons file: Beatrix Aldergate, age nine, vanished the night of the harvest moon. The last photograph in the file is a portrait — and the archive records show it was withdrawn by her own family. The beat is the first collision between Theo's skepticism and evidence he can't file away.

chapters.title: The House That Appraises Back
chapters.summary: POV Danny, the youngest crew member. Danny stays late to finish interior photos and finds the house has redecorated: walls papered with surveyor's reports, his own handwriting among them. The house knows them. He escapes at midnight, but his camera roll shows a girl in every frame, standing just behind him. The beat is the violation of being seen by something that wants you.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: POV Theo. The crew returns to the door and finds it open — a stairway descending into rooms that shouldn't fit beneath the lot. Marisol goes down first and doesn't come back up; her radio plays lullabies. Theo realizes the house has taken her the way it took Beatrix. The beat is guilt: they opened it, so it's theirs to close.

chapters.title: The Family That Locked the Door
chapters.summary: POV Theo, with the elderly neighbor Mrs. Okonkwo. She reveals the truth of 1974: Beatrix's parents, grieving her mother's death, walled the girl into the house's heart to keep her — and hid her portrait so no one could ever release her. The house has been feeding on kept things ever since. The beat is horror at human cruelty dressed up as love.

chapters.title: Loyalty Weighs More Than Truth
chapters.summary: POV Danny. Danny wants to call the police and run; Theo refuses to leave Marisol. Their argument splits the crew, and two workers quit, but the house won't let the quitters go — their cars circle the block, doors locked, until they come back. The beat is the theme sharpened: belonging to the house versus belonging to each other.

chapters.title: Down the Stairway
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Theo and Danny descend, moving through rooms that replay 1974 — a birthday party, a locked bedroom, a girl's voice counting to keep from crying. They find Marisol alive but half-remembered, already forgetting her mother's face. Beatrix appears, nine years old and fifty years old at once, and asks Theo the question that breaks him: why did everyone who loved her choose to keep her instead of free her? The beat is the climax's moral hinge.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: POV Theo. With the moon rising, Theo races to the county archive, steals the portrait back from a locked drawer his own appraisal credentials open, and returns as the house begins sealing its doors. He burns the portrait in the house's heart, telling Beatrix the truth: she was taken, it was wrong, and she is free to go. The house screams, Marisol wakes, and the walls begin to fall. The beat is love expressed as release, not keeping.

chapters.title: Appraised at Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Theo, epilogue. At dawn the lot is a clean foundation trench and an ordinary door lying flat in the dirt, hinges on the outside now. Marisol doesn't remember the house; Danny does, and stays. Theo files the appraisal — value: zero — and drives past the lot every harvest moon, leaving a single candle at the curb. The beat is quiet resolution: some doors you don't close, you just refuse to walk through again.
